exposure: urban sonic environment quality (pleasantness, evocative/inspiring role, space interactivity); area sound levels recorded 60-91 dB
behaviour_measure: self-reported attendance in the public open space (purpose of attendance, willingness to attend, accompanying friends/family)
key_finding: Sonic environment quality predicted people attendance on the historic pedestrian street: unpleasant sound conditions lowered willingness to attend and discouraged bringing friends and family, reinforcing individualistic use.

exposure: loudspeaker sound interventions in situ: bird song and water sound (natural), traffic noise and construction noise (artificial), plus quiet control and white noise
behaviour_measure: proportion of people engaging in social interaction, frequency of social interaction, percentage of time spent on social interaction
key_finding: Natural sound interventions raised the proportion of people engaged in social interaction by about 10% and increased interaction frequency and total duration by about 10%, mainly for within-group interactions, while noise interventions had no significant negative effect.
effect_stats: Natural sounds increase about 10% of people engaging in social interactions; natural sounds increase the total duration of social interactions by about 10%

exposure: natural and other sound sources (bird sounds, chirp/insect sounds, wind sounds) paired with visual landscape attributes (grassland, waterscape, woodland)
behaviour_measure: on-site mapping of visitors activities and activity vitality across landscape and sound settings (behaviour maps)
measurement_method: observation (on-site mapping) + self-report questionnaire for emotion
key_finding: Natural sounds (bird, chirp, wind) and nature-dominated visual landscapes were positively correlated with activity vitality; grasslands and woodlands attracted recreation and vitality became extremely high when paired with lakes.

exposure: played sound sources (grass-cutting noise, melodious music, no sound source) crossed with low/moderate/high thermal levels; LAeq and UTCI monitored
behaviour_measure: number of people (crowd flow), number of persons staying and staying time, approach/avoidance path choice relative to the sound source, walking speed
key_finding: Music attracted more visitors and slowed walking pace, whereas grass-cutting noise (especially under high temperature) reduced crowd flow, shortened staying time and produced avoidance paths away from the source.

design: mixed (field audio-visual measurement + questionnaire + regression modelling)
exposure: measured LAeq at 10 points with an expressway traffic-noise map and perceived sound sources; 77 dB identified as a critical threshold
behaviour_measure: behavioural vitality / activity intensity by functional zone and measurement point
key_finding: Lawn and pavement proportions and sound pressure level significantly affected behavioural vitality, with 77 dB acting as a critical threshold that separates distinct emotional prediction models.

exposure: perceived soundscape pleasantness and eventfulness in five urban parks; measured LAeq 3-min 43.9-67.7 dBA
behaviour_measure: self-reported static versus dynamic behaviour types and visit intensity (visit frequency, time of stay)
key_finding: Pleasant and eventful soundscapes promoted static behaviours (dynamic behaviours were driven only by eventfulness), and static behaviour in turn mediated the effect of soundscape characteristics on restorative experience, accounting for 8% of the total effect.
effect_stats: static behavior is the only mediating factor, accounting for 8% of the total effect

sample_n: NR (census commuting flows for Greater London and Brisbane)
exposure: modelled environmental noise levels (noise maps) intersected with commuting itineraries, together with built-environment density, land-use and amenity variables
behaviour_measure: commuting travel mode choice (walk, bicycle, car) and route-level noise exposure
measurement_method: secondary big data (census travel-to-work flows + modelled noise maps)
key_finding: Noise levels were among the relevant predictors of commuting mode choice in Greater London (crossing quieter roads mattered more than crossing loud ones) while built-environment characteristics dominated in Brisbane, and cycling patterned more like driving than like walking.

exposure: hidden-loudspeaker playback of light music (100.99 bpm) or highly annoying fan sound versus no sound, crossed with presence/absence of sewage odour on a 40 m x 4 m park walkway
behaviour_measure: crowd path position (approach to or recession from the source, ordinate y at path intersections), average crowd speed, duration time in the area
key_finding: Music attracted crowds toward the source, significantly reduced walking speed and increased duration, whereas fan sound and sewage odour drove crowds away, raised speed and shortened duration; odour strengthened the approach/recede trends but the positive effect of music exceeded the negative effect of odour.

exposure: dominant perceived sounds (sea waves, wind, traffic and other mechanical/anthropogenic sounds) and measured ambient LAeq (BSWA801; responses above 73 dBA excluded)
behaviour_measure: self-reported visit duration, visit frequency, visit purpose and activity intensity
key_finding: Behavioural patterns (visit duration, frequency and activity intensity) were significantly associated with all four perceived soundscape restorativeness components, and individual/behavioural factors outweighed sound characteristics in determining Fascination, Being-away and Compatibility.
